quote: Zeige, dass man durch aufeinanderfolgende beliebige An- wendung der Axiome niemals zu widersprechenden Sätzen gelangen kann.
english: Show that by successive arbitrary application of the axioms one can never arrive at contradictory theorems.
topic: Hilbert notes that all intersection-point theorems should follow from closure theorems, plans to list such theorems for circles, conics and quadrics, and sketches how to prove the consistency of the axioms by analytic means.

triage.modern_statement: Show that an axiom system, here Hilbert's axioms for (Euclidean) geometry, is consistent: no finite chain of deductions from the axioms yields both a statement and its negation. The page context ('by analytic means') points to a relative consistency proof by an analytic (coordinate) model. Such a model makes geometry consistent if the arithmetic of real or algebraic numbers is. This is the method Hilbert published in Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899). The general form of the question, consistency of arithmetic itself proved by finitary means, became Hilbert's 2nd Problem (1900) and later Hilbert's Programme.
triage.answered_by: Geometry: Hilbert himself, Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899). He built an analytic model over a countable field Ω of algebraic numbers (and over the reals), which proves geometry consistent relative to arithmetic. Arithmetic: posed as Hilbert's 2nd Problem in 1900. Gödel's second incompleteness theorem (1931) showed that a consistent system of this kind cannot prove its own consistency, which rules out a purely internal finitary proof. Gentzen (1936) proved Peano Arithmetic consistent using transfinite induction up to ε0. There is no consensus on whether these results settle the 2nd Problem.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899) proves consistency semantically. He presents an analytic model based on a field Ω of algebraic numbers, with real numbers as an alternative choice of coordinates.
If the arithmetic of real numbers is consistent, then Hilbert's system of axioms for geometry is consistent.
Hilbert's 2nd Problem (1900), the compatibility of the arithmetical axioms, asks for a proof that arithmetic is consistent. Hilbert notes that in geometry consistency is shown by building a model.

In the 1930s Gödel and Gentzen proved results that bear on the 2nd Problem. Gentzen published a consistency proof for Peano Arithmetic in 1936. There is no consensus on whether these results answer the problem.
Gentzen's 1936 proof shows that the consistency of first-order Peano Arithmetic can be proved over a weak base theory plus transfinite induction up to ε0.
Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931) showed that Hilbert's optimism about finitary consistency proofs was unfounded.

triage.why: The page context (consistency of axioms 'by analytic means', alongside geometry topics) matches Hilbert's work leading to Grundlagen der Geometrie. There he proved geometry consistent relative to arithmetic with an analytic model, which answers the note in its relative form. The wider demand, that no deductions from the axioms ever lead to a contradiction, became Hilbert's 2nd Problem. Gödel (1931) and Gentzen (1936) answered it in a limited, debated sense. Ordinal analysis and proof theory, which grew out of Gentzen's work, are still active research areas. I can't link the note to a specific date or to a particular one of these results from the sources alone, so tying it to Grundlagen is an inference from the page context.
